meta.theme: the gap between how much people are liked and how much they think they are liked explained as an inequality of evidence rather than as modesty or low self-regard, since each party hears their own commentary and sees only the other's manner, which makes the error one that self-persuasion cannot reach and that only a legible reaction closes

meta.reviewer_notes: Two explanations are set side by side and separated by what each predicts, so the passage's evidence paragraph does real adjudicating work. The three rivals — modesty as speech, harshness as a standard, and general unreliability in reading others — each own one option in all four questions, including the tone item, where they supply four different attitudes rather than two caricatures and a measured middle.

quality.adversarial_review: Three rivals run through all four questions. The first is modesty: the underestimate is a way of speaking rather than a belief. It is the passage's own opening candidate and dies on the anonymous slider, where nobody is listening and the gap survives, which is the sentence the evidence paragraph exists to deliver. The second, and the live rival, is severity: we judge ourselves by a harsher standard than we apply to others. It is attractive because the passage says we hear everything we did badly, and it is killed by the distinction the third paragraph draws in terms — the two parties are not applying different standards but reading different records, one of them private and unusually full of errors. The third is general unreliability, on which we simply cannot read other minds; it dies on the passage's insistence that the error has a direction and a size, and that it shrinks where the reaction becomes legible, neither of which a story about general inaccuracy predicts. On the vocabulary item the thesis in miniature has deliberately been placed in a distractor, so that the option which sounds most like the argument is the one that fails to define the word.

paragraphs.text: Two people leave a first conversation with rather different accounts of it. Each believes the other enjoyed it more than they did themselves, and each is wrong, and they are wrong by about the same amount. The finding is robust enough to have acquired a name, and the usual explanation for it is modesty: we are trained not to claim that we were charming, and what people report is the claim they are permitted to make rather than the belief they hold.

Modesty would predict certain things. It would predict that the gap closes when nobody is listening, that it is smaller among people who have been raised to speak well of themselves, and that it disappears altogether when the report is anonymous and costs nothing. None of that is what happens. Move the question to a private slider that no one else will see and the gap survives almost intact. It survives when people are asked to bet money on the answer. Whatever is going on, the participants are not managing an audience; they believe what they are reporting.

The likelier account is duller and harder to escape. In any conversation the two parties hold different records of it. You have access to a continuous inner commentary, which is largely a list of faults: the joke that landed a second late, the name you could not retrieve, the answer you gave to a question nobody asked. Of the other person you have only the outside, and the outside is solicitous by convention, because manners require the face to be pleasant whatever the mind is doing. So each of you compares a private ledger of errors against a public display of warmth, and reaches the obvious conclusion. It is not that we hold ourselves to a stricter standard than we hold others. It is that we are reading two different documents, and only one of them records the mistakes.

This is why the error is so resistant to advice. Being told that others like you more than you think cannot work, because it does not touch the evidence; the inner commentary keeps arriving and the other face keeps being polite, and a belief supported by everything you can observe is not dislodged by a statistic about people in general. What does close the gap is a reaction that becomes legible — a second meeting arranged, a message sent first, a piece of news somebody keeps for you. Notice that none of these is reassurance. They are simply occasions on which the other person's side of the record is made available, which is the one thing the first conversation could not supply.

questions.target_mistake: choosing the option that restates the passage's argument rather than the one that gives the word its sense in the clause where it appears
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: the word is explained by the clause that follows it, which is about manners requiring a pleasant face whatever the mind is doing.
questions.stem: In the third paragraph, “solicitous” is used to mean

options.A: anxious about the impression that one's own performance is making
options.B: trained by long practice to conceal what a person is really feeling
options.C: showing attentive concern for the comfort of the person one is with
options.D: kinder in what it shows than the private commentary running behind it

explanation.expert_notice: The word is glossed in the clause immediately after it: the outside is solicitous by convention, 'because manners require the face to be pleasant whatever the mind is doing'. Convention and manners point to an outward attentiveness to the other person, not to a state of mind.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the sense the sentence supports: an attentive, considerate manner directed at the person one is with. The passage needs exactly that meaning for its argument to work, since the point is that the visible half of the evidence is warm as a matter of form. A meaning about inner anxiety or concealment would make the face a report of feeling, which is what the sentence denies.
explanation.question_type_note: A word-in-context question is answered from the clause that surrounds the word, not from the argument the paragraph is making. Where an option summarises the passage instead of defining the word, it is answering a different question.
explanation.reading_habit: Cover the options and replace the word with your own, using only the clause it sits in. Then take the option nearest your word, not the one nearest the passage's thesis.

distractors.why_wrong: The word is close to solicitude in the sense of worry, which is a real sense of the family but not the one the clause licenses: the sentence is about what convention requires the face to do for the other person, and it belongs to the description of the outside rather than of any private state.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph is full of private anxiety — the late joke, the forgotten name — so a reading of the word as inward worry feels continuous with its surroundings.

distractors.why_wrong: Concealment is an inference a reader draws from the sentence rather than the meaning of the word in it. The passage says manners require a pleasant face whatever the mind is doing, which describes a convention that is followed openly, and being described as trained to hide feeling would make the same behaviour a deception.
distractors.seductive_element: It sits close to the argument's conclusion, that the visible half of the record is not a reliable report of what the other person thought.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the passage's thesis in miniature rather than a meaning: it describes the relation between the two records instead of saying what one word contributes to its sentence. Substituted into the sentence it produces a comparison the clause is not making.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the option that sounds most like the essay, and a reader who has understood the argument will hear the argument in it.

questions.target_mistake: keeping the explanation the passage opens with, or converting an inequality of evidence into a claim about self-esteem
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say beforehand: the two sides of a conversation hold unequal records, so the underestimate is an evidence problem rather than a problem of modesty or self-regard.
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: People speak of themselves more modestly than they privately believe, which is why they report having been liked rather less than they really were.
options.B: People are unreliable judges of what others make of them, and the impressions formed in a first conversation are worth very little.
options.C: Each party compares a private record of their own errors with the other’s display of warmth, so the gap is an inequality of evidence.
options.D: People hold themselves to a harsher standard than they hold anybody else, and a first conversation is where that severity is most visible.

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph gives the claim and then draws a line under it: 'It is not that we hold ourselves to a stricter standard than we hold others. It is that we are reading two different documents, and only one of them records the mistakes.' A passage that denies a rival in its own words is telling you where the main idea is not.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that denial stated positively. The asymmetry is in the material each party can see, not in the standard each applies, and the rest of the passage depends on it: the modesty account fails because the gap survives when nobody is listening, and advice fails because it leaves the evidence untouched. Only a reading about unequal records explains both of those results.
explanation.question_type_note: When a passage tests one explanation, discards it and installs another, the main idea is the replacement together with what it explains — never the explanation the first paragraph introduces.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what each candidate explanation predicts and check the prediction against the paragraph of evidence. The main idea of an essay of this shape is always the account that survives that check.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the explanation the passage introduces in order to test, and the second paragraph reports the test failing: the gap survives a private slider nobody will see and survives when people bet money on the answer. The passage concludes in terms that the participants believe what they report.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the first explanation offered and the most familiar one, and the passage states it sympathetically before taking it apart.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage describes an error with a direction and a known size, not a general incapacity, and it names the conditions under which the error shrinks. A claim that first impressions are worth very little would make the closing paragraph's legible reactions pointless.
distractors.seductive_element: Any finding that people are systematically wrong invites the larger and more quotable conclusion that people cannot read one another at all.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage denies this in a sentence written for the purpose. The two parties are not applying different standards; they are consulting different records, one of which happens to contain the errors. A difference of standard would survive the anonymous slider as easily as modesty fails to.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the near-tie: the list of remembered faults reads like self-criticism, and severity towards oneself is the moral people usually take from this finding.

questions.target_mistake: treating the remedy as a matter of persuasion, when the passage's account makes the belief a reasonable response to the evidence available
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: if the belief is supported by everything a person can observe, only new observation will move it, which is why reassurance cannot.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A person who is told the finding, and believes it, will go on underestimating how much a new acquaintance liked them.
options.B: A person who was brought up to speak well of themselves will show a noticeably smaller gap than other people do.
options.C: A person who dislikes the way they behaved in a conversation is applying to themselves a standard they would not apply to a stranger.
options.D: A person cannot know what a conversation meant to somebody else, so any estimate they form of it is guesswork.

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph states the mechanism of the failure rather than the fact of it: advice 'does not touch the evidence', because the commentary keeps arriving and the other face keeps being polite. A belief with undisturbed support is not moved by being contradicted.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that mechanism applied to one person. Knowing the finding adds a general statistic; it does not add a single observation about the particular person across the table, whose manner remains pleasant by convention and whose private record stays out of view. The passage says what would work instead, and it is always the arrival of new evidence rather than a change of mind.
explanation.question_type_note: Where a passage explains why a remedy fails, the inference to test is what happens to somebody who takes the remedy. Keep the author's mechanism and run the case through it.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says a belief is supported by the evidence available, expect the inference to be about what does and does not count as new evidence. Persuasion is not evidence.

distractors.why_wrong: This is one of the predictions the passage lists on behalf of the modesty account and then reports as not borne out, along with the private slider and the wager. Taking it as an inference requires the explanation the second paragraph spends its length removing.
distractors.seductive_element: It is stated inside the passage as a prediction, which makes it look like a claim the passage endorses rather than one it tests.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage sets its account against exactly this one: we are not holding ourselves to a stricter standard, we are reading a different document. A person who winces at their own conversation has seen faults that were never visible in anybody else's, which is a difference of access rather than of severity.
distractors.seductive_element: The catalogue of small failures in the third paragraph is written in the voice of self-reproach, and self-reproach is usually explained by high standards.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage treats the estimate as wrong in a particular direction by a measurable amount, and names circumstances in which it improves. Guesswork would have no direction and no remedy, and the closing paragraph offers one.
distractors.seductive_element: The argument does turn on how little of the other person is visible, which makes a sweeping conclusion about unknowable minds feel like the next sentence.

questions.target_mistake: hearing a finding that flatters the reader as encouragement, when the author declines to offer it as comfort and says why comfort would not work
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before the options: the writing is amused by the symmetry of the mistake and pointedly refuses to turn it into reassurance.
questions.stem: The author's tone in the passage is best described as

options.A: encouraging, keen that the reader should take the finding personally and be cheered by it
options.B: clinical and uninvolved, reporting results without any interest in what they feel like
options.C: sceptical throughout, doubtful that any of these effects have really been established
options.D: amused by the symmetry of the mistake, and unwilling to turn it into consolation

explanation.expert_notice: Two things fix the voice. The comedy of the third paragraph — the joke that landed a second late, the answer to a question nobody asked — and the flat refusal in the fourth: 'Notice that none of these is reassurance.' The writing enjoys the situation and declines to soothe.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps both. The symmetry that opens the passage, two people wrong in the same direction by the same amount, is presented as a small comedy, and the author writes about the inner commentary with evident pleasure in its detail. But the closing paragraph withholds the comforting use of the finding and explains why it would fail, which is the opposite of what a reassuring essay would do with the same material.
explanation.question_type_note: Tone is fixed by what an author does with a fact, not by the subject. A cheerful finding handled without warmth and a grim one handled kindly are both common; read the verbs and the asides.
explanation.reading_habit: Find the sentence where the author could have consoled the reader and did not, or could have condemned and did not. The road not taken tells you more about the voice than the adjectives do.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph is written against this use of the finding: being told that others like you more than you think 'cannot work, because it does not touch the evidence'. An author trying to cheer the reader would end on the statistic rather than on the reasons it will not help.
distractors.seductive_element: The content is flattering — you are better liked than you believe — and readers hear flattery in the voice of whoever reports it.

distractors.why_wrong: Detachment does not describe writing that stops to enumerate the joke that landed late and the name that would not come. The passage is interested in exactly what the experience feels like from inside, and it uses that interest as evidence.
distractors.seductive_element: The essay is argumentative and quotes findings, and a reader who registers only the structure will call the voice neutral.

distractors.why_wrong: The author's scepticism is aimed at one explanation, not at the finding, which is called robust in the first paragraph and used without hesitation in the last. What is doubted is modesty as a cause, and the doubt is settled with evidence rather than left open.
distractors.seductive_element: The second paragraph is a sustained demolition, and a reader who meets a demolition early takes doubt for the prevailing attitude.

vocabulary.passage_use: the outside is solicitous by convention
vocabulary.meaning_here: showing attentive concern for another person's comfort

vocabulary.passage_use: compares a private ledger of errors against a public display of warmth
vocabulary.meaning_here: a running record in which items are entered one by one
plain enough to be read off without interpretation

mentor.challenge: A familiar finding is given a familiar explanation in the first paragraph, and the second paragraph takes that explanation apart. Keep track of which account is on trial and which is doing the judging.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: People leave a conversation believing they were liked less than they were because each party compares a private record full of their own small errors with the other person's outwardly pleasant manner, which makes the mistake an inequality of evidence rather than modesty or self-criticism.
mentor.main_idea: The usual explanation is modesty, but the gap survives when reports are private and even when money is at stake, so it is a belief rather than a performance. The better account is that each side of a conversation sees different material: your own faults in detail, the other person's manner only. That is why reassurance does not help and why a concrete reaction does.
mentor.simple_explanation:
After a first conversation, both people usually think the other one enjoyed it more. Both are wrong, by roughly the same amount.

The usual explanation is modesty: we are not supposed to say we were charming, so we say we were not. But if modesty were the cause, the gap would disappear when nobody is watching. It does not. Ask people privately, on a slider nobody else sees, and the gap is still there. Offer them money to get it right and it is still there. So they are not performing. They really believe it.

The better explanation is simpler. During the conversation you can hear your own thoughts, and those thoughts are mostly a list of things that went slightly wrong: the joke that came out a second too late, the name you forgot, the answer to a question nobody asked. Of the other person you can see only the outside, and the outside is polite, because manners require a pleasant face.

So you are comparing your own faults with somebody else's good manners, and the comparison comes out badly. It is not that you judge yourself more harshly. It is that you are reading two different documents, and only one of them lists the mistakes.

This explains why being told the fact does not help. The next conversation still gives you your own commentary and still shows you a polite face. What does help is something you can actually observe: a second meeting arranged, a message sent first, a piece of news saved for you. Those are not compliments. They are pieces of the other person's record finally becoming visible.
mentor.why_difficult: The difficulty is not the vocabulary but the closeness of two explanations that sound almost the same. Reading a private list of one's own faults against a stranger's pleasant manner looks very like being hard on oneself, and the passage spends one deliberate sentence separating them. Readers who miss that sentence will carry a self-esteem reading into every question, and it will fit the options that were built for it. The passage also asks the reader to notice that what refutes modesty is a prediction failing, not an assertion.
mentor.author_intention: To replace a comfortable explanation of a well-known finding with a duller one that actually predicts the evidence, and to explain, without offering any comfort, why the mistake does not respond to being pointed out.

paragraph_journey.note: Two people leave a conversation each thinking the other liked it more. Both are wrong by about the same amount, and modesty is the usual explanation.
If modesty were the cause the gap would vanish when nobody is watching. It does not, even with money on it. So people believe what they say.
You hear all your own small failures and see only the other person's good manners. Different records, not different standards.
Advice fails because it adds no evidence. What closes the gap is something visible, like a second meeting or a message sent first.

mentor.tone_progression: Light and faintly comic while the finding is laid out, briskly forensic through the paragraph that dismantles modesty, and dry at the close, where the author points out that the things which actually help are not reassurance and does not offer any.
key_transitions: 'Modesty would predict certain things.' (paragraph 2) — an explanation is turned into a set of testable claims.
'It is not that we hold ourselves to a stricter standard than we hold others.' (paragraph 3) — the sentence separating the author's account from its nearest rival.
'Notice that none of these is reassurance.' (paragraph 4) — the refusal that fixes the tone of the whole piece.
mentor.misunderstanding: The common misreading turns the passage into an essay about low self-esteem: we are hard on ourselves, and the remedy is to be kinder. Everything in the third paragraph's list of small failures encourages it, and the passage blocks it with a single sentence that a hurried reader skims, because the two accounts predict the same feeling and differ only in what causes it. A second misreading takes modesty for the author's view, since it is stated first and stated well.
mentor.traps_summary: Two shapes recur. One is an explanation the passage introduces in order to test, offered back as though the passage endorsed it. The other is a near neighbour of the thesis — a stricter standard instead of a fuller record — which sounds identical until you ask what each would predict. Options that widen the claim into a general statement about unknowable minds are the third.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage sets two explanations of the same fact side by side, do not choose by plausibility. Write down what each one predicts, then find the paragraph where the author checks a prediction, because that paragraph is the argument and everything before it is only staging. The same habit protects you from the commonest trap in this kind of essay, which is an option quoting the explanation that was put up to be knocked down.
mentor.real_world: The same asymmetry runs through job interviews, first days at work and any performance where you can hear yourself rehearsing: you hold a detailed record of your own stumbles and a polite summary of everybody else's opinion.
mentor.takeaway: You are comparing your rehearsal notes with somebody else's manners, and the comparison was never fair.
mentor.reflection_question: What would you have to see, rather than be told, before you believed that a conversation went better than it felt?
